sources.claim: BuzzFeed News feature (12 January 2018) on transgender women in French prisons: under Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code men and women are held in separate establishments, so trans women whose legal gender is marked male (the vast majority, without sex-reassignment surgery) are placed in men's facilities; a detainee recalled inmates shouting 'We don't want any women here!' and threats of violence; Adeline Hazan, controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, says transgender detainees — overwhelmingly women — are the group that suffers the most in prison, illustrated by American trans woman Kara B. held in 'worrying' conditions. National prison-placement framework; no division-specific detail for this region.

CGLPL (French national preventive mechanism) opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty (follow-up to its opinion of 30 June 2010): it records the persistence of serious violations of trans detainees' fundamental rights in adult prisons, while none were noted in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres; the review covered the situations of some forty transgender detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man, and inspection visits at the Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station. National custodial-inspection framework; no division-specific finding for this region.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed News feature (12 Jan 2018), 'The Plight Of Trans Women In Prison': transgender women incarcerated in France on the basis of their legal gender fall into a legal grey area and are punished for far more than their alleged crimes - first-person accounts of placement in an all-male facility (a three-day stay in Lille's men's prison in 2014, with detainee and staff hostility; an Argentinian trans woman's story of incarceration); Article D248 of the criminal procedure code assigns detainees by the sex on their ID; the controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty says transgender detainees are the group that 'suffers the most' in prison; also covers the well-publicised case of a US trans woman detained in poor conditions after a 2016 Paris protest case.

Opinion of 25 May 2021 of the Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté (CGLPL), unofficial English translation: official inspectorate opinion on the treatment of transgender persons in ALL places of deprivation of liberty; built on about forty referrals received since 2010, interviews with trans associations and European experts, and five on-site inspections (Fleury-Mérogis men's and women's prisons, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse-Seysses and the Toulouse central police station - eight trans women and one trans man interviewed); finds persistent serious violations of fundamental rights of trans detainees, isolation and overcrowding risks; recommends that the 2016 depathologising law (no more surgery requirement for civil-status change) be translated into prison regulations; explicitly extends to intersex and non-binary people.

sources.title: LGBT rights in France - Wikipedia
sources.claim: The national framework this Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes record stands under: France legalised same-sex marriage and full adoption in 2013 (civil solidarity pacts since 1999), Penal Code article 225-1 has covered 'gender identity' since an 18 November 2016 amendment that replaced 'sexual identity' (protected since 2012), and homophobic hate speech has carried penalties up to EUR 45,000 and/or one year's imprisonment since a 31 December 2004 amendment. On legal gender recognition, a bill approved by the Senate on 6 November 2015 and by the National Assembly on 24 May 2016 was signed into law on 18 November 2016 and took effect on 1 January 2017: it abolished the sex-reassignment-surgery and forced-sterilisation requirements, rejected a Senate amendment that would have demanded proof of medical treatment, and requires going before a court rather than any medical intervention; transsexualism is classed under long-term-illness ALD 31, so gender-affirming treatment is funded by the Sécurité Sociale. It supplies the concrete national rules on documents, protection and care that a trans visitor to Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes encounters and grounds the record's at-national-score assessment, since the region's own page carries no trans-specific content.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed feature (Rozenn Le Carboulec) on trans women in French prisons: Article D248 of the Criminal Procedure Code mandates separate establishments for men and women, so placement follows the sex on identity documents and trans women are typically held in men's facilities - as of 1 Nov 2016 there were 13 transgender detainees held across eight establishments, most at Fleury-Mérogis. Profiles Paola, an Argentine trans woman transferred to a men's facility in 2014 and met with shouts of 'We don't want any women here', despite a passport listing her as female, because French law does not recognise her Argentine legal gender for placement purposes. Documents inconsistent access to treatment and a 2,000-euro symbolic damages award over detention conditions, with the justice minister pressed to amend D248.

Opinion of the Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté (CGLPL), France's national preventive mechanism, dated 25 May 2021, on the care of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: building on referrals received since 2010 and a 2010 opinion on transsexual prisoners, it covers all places of deprivation of liberty. Inspections cited include Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station, with evidence from eight transgender women; it documents discrimination, stigmatisation and health/social-care blind spots and recommends policies to combat the discrimination and exclusion they face, referencing law n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016 on justice modernisation/prison transfers and the 'racism, antisemitism, LGBT and discrimination' referents appointed since 2018. This is the basis for the record's claim that the CGLPL reports persistent serious violations of trans detainees' rights across inspected prisons.

records.name: Mimaropa
records.current_summary:
Mimaropa carries no region-specific laws against transgender people: no provincial ordinance criminalising expression or facility use is documented, and the framework that applies here is the national one — same-sex relations are legal, legal gender recognition does not exist, national equality bills have been filed repeatedly for decades without passing, while some cities and provinces have enacted local non-discrimination ordinances. Public homophobic and transphobic slurs are criminalised by the Safe Spaces Act, and school anti-bullying and gender-responsive education policies cover sexual orientation and gender identity.

Public acceptance is partial: a 2018 national survey found roughly one in five behind same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets, and executive orders creating a national diversity-and-inclusion programme remained unimplemented as of 2025 according to audited reporting. In mid-2025 a cluster of killings of trans people across several other provinces — a student found in a northern river, an activist shot in a southern city, another woman killed in the capital region — drew national calls to pass the stalled equality bill, documenting a pattern of lethal violence against a backdrop of unenacted protection. For a visitor, Mimaropa's profile is the national one: no state penalty for being trans, courts and local ordinances as practical recourse, and physical safety conditioned on setting and discretion.

sources.claim: Outright International (IGLHRC) Philippines country overview (updated 2025): same-sex relations are legal and acceptance indices rank the country among the most accepting in Asia, but trans people cannot access legal gender recognition - the 2001 Clerical Error Law (RA 9048) blocks gender-marker correction - and national non-discrimination bills filed since 1999 remain unenacted, with two civil-union bills filed since 2022 facing religious-conservative opposition; non-discrimination ordinances exist at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels. A 2018 SWS survey found only 22% of Filipinos supported same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets. The Safe Spaces Act criminalises homophobic and transphobic slurs; the Anti-Bullying Act and the Gender-Responsive Basic Education Policy (reiterated 2022, June designated Pride Month) cover sexual orientation and gender identity in schools; Executive Orders No. 100 (2019) and No. 51 (2023) creating the national Diversity and Inclusion Program remain unimplemented as of 2025.

Bulatlat (26 Jun 2025): 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol, a Cagayan State University business-management student, was found dead in a Cagayan province river on 23 June 2025 days after being reported missing, with signs of physical assault; a criminology student who admitted driving her surrendered to police while denying involvement. A second killing that same day - trans woman and former activist-journalist Ali Macalintal shot by an unidentified gunman inside an acupuncture clinic in General Santos - is reported alongside, and Bahaghari and other groups cite the cases in calling for passage of the SOGIESC Equality Bill, stuck in Congress for 25 years (latest version Senate Bill 1600), which would prohibit admission denial, denial of public and health services, and infliction of physical harm or verbal abuse based on SOGIE.

sources.claim: International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (last updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal nationwide, no legal gender recognition, LGBTI organisations can register; the country ranks among the most 'accepting' in the region in perception indices and surveys show strong support for an anti-discrimination law, but a 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found only 22% of Filipinos supported same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets; diversity-and-inclusion executive orders (2019, amended 2023) exist but were not implemented as of 2025; non-discrimination ordinances enacted at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels, while national SOGIE legislation has been filed repeatedly since 1999 but never passed; Anti-Bullying Act 2013 and the Gender-Responsive Basic Education Policy (2017, reiterated 2022) cover SOGI in schools; Safe Spaces Act 2019 covers homophobic and transphobic slurs.

Bulatlat news (26 June 2025): an eighteen-year-old trans woman (Kierra Apostol, student of Cagayan State University, Peñablanca) was found dead in a Cagayan province river on 23 June 2025 with visible signs of physical assault; a person who admitted picking her up the previous night surrendered to police and denied killing her; the same piece records the killing of trans activist and former journalist Ali Macalintal by an unidentified gunman inside an acupuncture clinic in General Santos (23 June) and of Shalani Dolina in Caloocan earlier in 2025; a national LGBT alliance says the violence is 'proof that LGBT persons remain unsafe' and demands passage of the SOGIESC Equality Bill, stuck in Congress for 25 years (latest version filed 2022 as House Bill 5551 / Senate Bill 1600).

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in the Philippines - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia's national overview supplies the framework a visitor to the Zamboanga Peninsula stands under: non-commercial, private, consensual same-sex activity is legal in the Philippines, but transgender people cannot change their legal gender, the Family Code defines marriage as between a man and a woman, and there is no national anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity (only an anti-bullying law in basic education and a still-pending SOGIE Equality Bill). The page's local-ordinance section names Zamboanga City - the peninsula's regional center - among the 20+ local governments with their own anti-discrimination ordinances, listing Zamboanga City's as enacted in 2020 (cited to a Daily Tribune report of 28 December 2020), so the local legal floor in the region includes this SOGIE protection.

records.name: Eastern Visayas
records.current_summary: This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier, which identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02); it is therefore assessed at the national score. The attached sources are national-level rather than regional: a country-organisation overview of the national legal picture, a June 2025 report on the killing of an 18-year-old trans woman in a different province (Cagayan), and a national news item on a case in another region (Batangas) that could not be retrieved at fetch time.

sources.claim: Outright International's Philippines country overview (updated 12 March 2026): same-sex conduct legal nationwide; no legal gender recognition (still required: no LGR pathway); Executive Order 100 s.2019 (signed 17 Dec 2019) created a Diversity and Inclusion Program, amended by EO 51 s.2023 to add a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee, neither implemented as of 2025; anti-discrimination ordinances exist at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels but national legislation filed since 1999 has not been enacted; a 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found 22% support for same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets.

Alternative-media report (26 June 2025): an 18-year-old trans woman, Kierra Apostol, was found dead with signs of physical assault in a river in Peñablanca, Cagayan province on 23 June 2025 after being missing since 22 June; her mother reported the disappearance to local police; Bahaghari (national LGBT alliance) chairperson called the killing part of a pattern of violence against Filipino trans women and renewed calls for the SOGIESC Equality Bill. Case is in Cagayan Valley region, not Eastern Visayas — national-climate evidence.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in the Philippines - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia's LGBTQ rights in the Philippines page is the national-framework document a visitor stands under in Eastern Visayas (national law applies uniformly across the region's six provinces) and it records the only Eastern-Visayas-specific datapoints located: in Northern Samar, two of the province's 24 municipalities were reported (circa 2012) to be run by openly LGBTQ mayors, and Leyte is among the provinces listed as having LGBTQ elected officials. The page also fixes the national legal baseline for the region: there is no general anti-discrimination law at national level while numerous LGU-level SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances exist elsewhere in the country, transgender people may not change their legal gender, same-sex marriage is not recognized (the Family Code defines marriage as between 'a man and a woman'), and the SOGIE Equality Bill has remained pending in Congress since the 2000s. This confirms the record's assessment that Eastern Visayas shows local LGBTQ political participation but no legal deviation from the national position.
